text:
The war with Iran ended this morning, or it didn’t, depending on which government you ask.

Donald Trump posted on Truth Social at approximately 10 AM that the deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is “now complete,” that he has authorized the toll-free opening of the Strait of Hormuz, and that the US naval blockade is simultaneously removed. He closed with “Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow!” Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, who mediated the negotiations, confirmed a peace deal has been reached and that both sides have declared the immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon. A signing ceremony is scheduled for Switzerland on June 19.

Iran’s military, within the same news cycle, issued a statement declaring that it had “humiliated” the United States and Israel, that American and Zionist enemies have been forced to accept defeat and surrender, and that Iran’s armed forces imposed their “divine and iron will” on the outcome. The Iranian deputy foreign minister said the agreement “was not just a product of diplomacy but also owed to Iran’s military achievements.”

So: the deal is done, and it is a historic American victory, and it is also a humiliating American defeat, and both of these descriptions were issued within hours of each other about the same document.

This is not a minor discrepancy in emphasis. This is two governments announcing peace while describing different wars. The question of what is actually in the agreement is not academic. As recently as Friday, Trump was on Truth Social calling Iran’s account of the deal terms a statement that “bears no relation to the truth.” Iran had been circulating a 14-point draft that included a commitment from the US to lift oil sanctions, the release of half of Iran’s frozen funds before final negotiations begin, withdrawal of all US forces from Iran, and a reconstruction package worth at least $300 billion. Trump said those terms had nothing to do with what was agreed to in writing. Iran said that was the document. Neither side produced the document.

The Times of Israel is reporting this morning that the deal likely returns the region to the status that existed before the war, but with thousands of people dead and Iran wielding new negotiating leverage from its demonstrated ability to close the Strait. If accurate, that is the strategic summary: the US went to war, conducted a bombing campaign, imposed a naval blockade, threatened to destroy Iranian civilization, and emerged with approximately the situation it started with, minus the dead and plus Iran’s enhanced regional credibility. Trump is calling this a win. Iran is calling this a win. Somebody is lying, and the most charitable interpretation is that both sides are telling their domestic audiences a version of events that their domestic audiences can survive.

None of this is surprising if you have been watching this administration manage information. The pattern from the Haberman and Swan reporting on the Epstein situation applies here at civilizational scale: announce the resolution loudly, manage the terms quietly, and hope the gap between the announcement and the reality closes before anyone counts the distance. The announcement is the product. The deal is secondary.

What is certain: the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil supply moves, was closed. Global markets were rattled for weeks. A naval blockade was imposed and maintained. Strikes were threatened, called off, threatened again. Pakistan mediated. Switzerland will host the signing. The European powers, Britain, France, Germany, and Italy, announced this morning they are prepared to lift sanctions on Iran in exchange for steps on its nuclear program, which tells you something about what the deal’s actual architecture probably looks like, since European sanctions relief is exactly the kind of concession that appears nowhere in Trump’s victory lap and prominently in Iran’s version of the document.

The war is over, conditionally, pending a signing that has not happened, between two parties who are already disputing the terms of the thing they just agreed to. The Strait may open on a timeline that one side says is immediate and the other side says is thirty days. The nuclear program, which was the stated justification for the war, is addressed in a framework that nobody has released and both sides are characterizing in contradictory ways. Israel, whose interests were supposedly central to the entire operation, was not included in the negotiations and has not commented.

The chaos is not a bug in the process. It is the process. This is what dealmaking looks like when the deal-maker’s primary product is the announcement rather than the agreement, when the press release is the deliverable and the details are for later, when “Ships of the World, start your engines” is a Truth Social post rather than a verified operational order to the Navy. Whether the ships actually move, whether the blockade actually lifts, whether the signing in Switzerland produces a document both governments will sign with the same understanding of what it says: those are questions for next week.

Today the war ended. Probably. Both sides won. Allegedly. The terms are agreed. Reportedly. Start your engines.
